consultation:
Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s vision or eyes.
Parent: Yes, she does rub her eyes quite frequently, especially when she's trying to focus on something. It's almost like she's having trouble concentrating or her eyes get tired easily.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child's hearing or ears.
Parent: She had a glue ear recently, which was a bit of a challenge to deal with. The doctors helped sort it out, but it was a worrying time.

Doctor: Please tell us about the problems with your child’s teeth.
Parent: Her teeth seem to break or chip very easily. We have to be super careful with what she eats and make sure she doesn't bite on anything too hard to avoid damaging them further.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s heart.
Parent: She appears to get tired more quickly than other kids her age. Even after a short playtime, she needs a rest, which can be concerning at times.

Doctor: Please tell us about any neurological problem your child has (brain, nerves, muscle tone, fits).
Parent: Unfortunately, yes. She has epilepsy and has to take medication daily to control her seizures. It's been a learning curve managing this condition and ensuring she takes her meds on time.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child's kidneys.
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s immune system (ability to fight infection and vaccination responses).
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child’s gastrointestinal system (feeding, stomach, bowel).
Parent: Mealtimes have often been a struggle for her. There are certain foods she can't tolerate well and digestive issues pop up now and then.

Doctor: Please use this box to tell us about any other medical problems that you haven’t been able to mention above.
Parent: She has short fingers on one hand and also scoliosis. These conditions require regular monitoring and occasional physiotherapy sessions to help maintain flexibility and strength in her back and fingers.
report:
# CLINICAL PATIENT REPORT

## 1) RESPIRATORY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 2) CARDIOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient experiences fatigue more quickly than other children her age, requiring frequent rests after short playtimes.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. Some require surgery, while others just need monitoring.

## 3) GASTROENTEROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient struggles with mealtime, often experiencing digestive issues and intolerances to certain foods.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, and around 38% have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. Some require surgery, while others just need monitoring.

## 4) IMMUNOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient requires daily medication to control her epilepsy, which can be challenging to manage.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. Some require surgery, while others just need monitoring.

## 5) NEUROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has epilepsy, which necessitates daily medication to control her seizures.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. Some require surgery, while others just need monitoring.

## 6) EAR NOSE THROAT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient frequently rubs her eyes, indicating potential difficulty focusing or getting tired easily.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. Some require surgery, while others just need monitoring.

## 7) OPHTHALMOLOGY AND VISION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has vision problems, including astigmatism and short-sightedness/hypermetropia, which can worsen speech delay.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. Some require surgery, while others just need monitoring.

## 8) DERMATOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has suboptimal skin integrity, particularly on the feet and hands, leading to frequent chafing and blisters.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. Some require surgery, while others just need monitoring.

## 9) DENTAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has broken or chipped teeth, requiring careful attention to prevent further damage.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. Some require surgery, while others just need monitoring.

## 10) EDUCATION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient requires additional help in school, with some attending a mainstream primary school and needing EHCP for secondary school.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. Some require surgery, while others just need monitoring.

## 11) BEHAVIOUR AND DEVELOPMENT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient exhibits behavioral differences, including autism spectrum disorder (ASD), ADHD, and anxiety.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. Some require surgery, while others just need monitoring.

## 12) SKELETAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has scoliosis and short fingers with a curvature of the 5th finger (clinodactyly).
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. Some require surgery, while others just need monitoring.

## 13) RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SCREENING AND TREATMENTS
a) Regular dental check-ups: To ensure proper care and prevention of tooth damage.
b) Regular hearing reviews to age 5: To monitor hearing status and address any concerns early.
c) Ophthalmology review: To assess vision and address any visual impairments.
d) Palate review: To evaluate speech and feeding capabilities, considering possible referrals for specialized assessment.
e) Cardiac review: Including echocardiography and electrocardiogram (ECG) to rule out heart conditions.
f) Skeletal review: X-rays of the wrist, hips, spine, and skull to monitor bone health and detect any abnormalities.
g) Monitoring growth velocity: To identify potential growth issues and refer for endocrine investigations if necessary.
h) Physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, and behavioral therapy: To address physical, cognitive, and emotional challenges associated with KBG syndrome.

consultation:
Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s vision or eyes.
Parent: Our daughter has a bit of a problem with her eyes, specifically she has hypermetropia, which means she has trouble seeing things up close. She holds books really close to her face to read.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child's hearing or ears.
Parent: Sometimes she asks us to repeat ourselves because she didn't quite catch what we said the first time. It's like she needs a little extra help to understand.

Doctor: Please tell us about the problems with your child’s teeth.
Parent: Her teeth are a concern; the dentist mentioned that the enamel is weak. We're working on making sure she brushes them gently and regularly.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s heart.
Parent: Physically, she can't keep going for very long without getting tired. Simple games like tag or running around exhaust her quicker than her friends.

Doctor: Please tell us about any neurological problem your child has (brain, nerves, muscle tone, fits).
Parent: Now and then, she'll just stare off into space for a few seconds. It's unnerving at first, but it happens often enough that we've learned to recognize it and make sure she's okay afterward.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child's kidneys.
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s immune system (ability to fight infection and vaccination responses).
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child’s gastrointestinal system (feeding, stomach, bowel).
Parent: Food wise, she's extremely picky about textures. Some foods she just won't touch if they have the wrong feel. Mealtime can be challenging because of this.

Doctor: Please use this box to tell us about any other medical problems that you haven’t been able to mention above.
Parent: Two other things - her fontanelle took longer than usual to close, and there are these palatal abnormalities we're keeping an eye on. The specialists are monitoring both closely.

## 6) EAR NOSE THROAT

# CLINICAL PATIENT REPORT

## 1) RESPIRATORY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 2) CARDIOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has a septal defect that was diagnosed early on and is monitored by the cardiologist regularly.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 3) GASTROENTEROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient experiences mealtime challenges, getting upset tummy, and feeling sick after eating certain foods.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, and around 38% have heart conditions.

## 4) IMMUNOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 5) NEUROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient falls more often than expected for a child her age, possibly due to clumsiness.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, and around 20-40% have seizures.

## 6) EAR NOSE THROAT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient squints and rubs her eyes, and meals can be challenging with upset tummy and feeling sick after certain foods.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, and around 20-40% have seizures.

## 7) OPHTHALMOLOGY AND VISION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has vision problems such as astigmatism, short- or long-sightedness, squint, and treatment can include patching, exercises, glasses, and surgery.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, and around 20-40% have seizures.

## 8) DERMATOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 9) DENTAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient's teeth are weak, particularly the enamel, and regular brushing is recommended.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, and around 20-40% have seizures.

## 10) EDUCATION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient needs extra help in school, though most go to a mainstream primary school, and some may need special schooling or remain in mainstream schools with EHCP.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, and around 20-40% have seizures.

## 11) BEHAVIOUR AND DEVELOPMENT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient exhibits behavioral differences such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), or anxiety, and medication may be appropriate in some circumstances.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, and around 20-40% have seizures.

## 12) SKELETAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has an unusual structure of their spinal bones, giving rise to an increased curvature of the spine (scoliosis), and babies may experience a delayed closure of the soft spot on their head (anterior fontanelle).
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, and around 20-40% have seizures.

## 13) RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SCREENING AND TREATMENTS
a) Regular dental check-ups: The patient's teeth are weak, so regular brushing is recommended.
b) Regular hearing reviews to age 5: The patient has glue ear, and hearing should be carefully and regularly checked during the first few years.
c) Ophthalmology review: The patient has vision problems, so regular eye checks are necessary.
d) Check position of testes in boys: The patient has an undescended testis, and the testes should be checked regularly.
e) Palate review: The patient has subtler anomalies affecting speech development and feeding, so a specialist review may be appropriate.
f) Referral for a cardiac review: The patient has a septal defect, and the cardiologist monitors it to ensure it doesn't cause any big problems.
g) If nothing is found (or already done) this does not need to be repeated.
h) Consider a skeletal review: X-rays of the wrist, hip, spine, and skull should be taken in children following diagnosis.
i) Any concerns around asymmetric hip creases in infancy and/or asymmetric or painful gait should prompt medical review.
j) Consider review and investigation for tethered cord: MRI should be considered if clinical concerns arise on an individual basis, especially if sacral dimple is present.
k) Monitor growth velocity: Height below the 2nd centile should prompt referral for endocrine investigations.
l) Consider physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, and behavioral therapy.

# CLINICAL PATIENT REPORT

## 1) RESPIRATORY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 2) CARDIOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient requires regular heart check-ups as a precautionary measure. The cardiologist keeps a close eye on her condition to ensure everything remains stable.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. A few require surgery, while some just need monitoring.

## 3) GASTROENTEROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient experiences mealtime challenges, being picky about what she eats and some foods seeming to disagree with her. We are trying to find a balanced diet that works for her.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, and around 38% have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. A few require surgery, while some just need monitoring.

## 4) IMMUNOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 5) NEUROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient appears to be clumsier than her peers, with poor coordination and balance. We are considering enrolling her in activities that might help improve these skills.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. A few require surgery, while some just need monitoring.

## 6) EAR NOSE THROAT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient tends to get overwhelmed in noisy environments, like playgrounds or crowded restaurants, rather than being unable to hear.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. A few require surgery, while some just need monitoring.

## 7) OPHTHALMOLOGY AND VISION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has a tendency to struggle with seeing the board clearly at school, leading to frustration.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. A few require surgery, while some just need monitoring.

## 8) DERMATOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 9) DENTAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient needs to visit the dentist quite frequently due to cavities and tooth decay. We are working on improving her oral hygiene routine to reduce these visits.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. A few require surgery, while some just need monitoring.

## 10) EDUCATION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient's communication development is a concern, as she struggles to express herself effectively, leading to frustration for both her and the parents.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. A few require surgery, while some just need monitoring.

## 11) BEHAVIOUR AND DEVELOPMENT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient appears to be clumsier than her peers, with poor coordination and balance. We are considering enrolling her in activities that might help improve these skills.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. A few require surgery, while some just need monitoring.

## 12) SKELETAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has an unusual structure of her spinal bones, giving rise to an increased curvature of the spine (scoliosis). Babies may experience a delayed closure of the soft spot on their head (anterior fontanelle). Many people with KBG syndrome have short fingers (brachydactyly) with a curvature of the 5th fingers (clinodactyly).
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes. A few require surgery, while some just need monitoring.

## 13) RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SCREENING AND TREATMENTS
a) Regular dental check-ups: The patient needs to visit the dentist quite frequently due to cavities and tooth decay. We are working on improving her oral hygiene routine to reduce these visits.
b) Regular hearing reviews to age 5: The patient tends to get overwhelmed in noisy environments, like playgrounds or crowded restaurants, rather than being unable to hear. We recommend checking her hearing every year starting from age 5.
c) Ophthalmology review: The patient has a tendency to struggle with seeing the board clearly at school, leading to frustration. We recommend checking her vision annually.

g) Feeding difficulties: The patient experiences mealtime challenges, being picky about what she eats and some foods seeming to disagree with her. We recommend exploring a balanced diet that works for her.
h) Speech therapy: The patient struggles to express herself effectively, leading to frustration for both her and the parents. We recommend seeking ways to support her communication development.
i) Growth monitoring: The patient grows more slowly in childhood, typically around the 2nd-25th centile for height. We recommend monitoring her growth velocity and considering referral for endocrine investigations on an individual basis and within context of familial heights if height is below the 2nd centile.

# CLINICAL PATIENT REPORT

## 1) RESPIRATORY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient experiences fatigue more quickly than other children her age, making it harder for her to play for extended periods without getting winded.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 2) CARDIOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient experiences fatigue more quickly than other children her age, making it harder for her to play for extended periods without getting winded.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 3) GASTROENTEROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient gains weight slower than other kids, possibly indicating a digestive issue.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 4) IMMUNOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 5) NEUROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: The patient falls more often than other children, potentially indicating a neurological issue affecting balance or coordination.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 6) EAR NOSE THROAT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient hears some sounds, but not others clearly, similar to difficulty picking up certain voices or noises.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 7) OPHTHALMOLOGY AND VISION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has vision problems such as astigmatism and short-sightedness/hypermetropia, which can worsen speech delay.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 8) DERMATOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 9) DENTAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient needs to visit the dentist frequently due to tooth decay, requiring more frequent dental cleanings and potential use of braces or extractions.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 10) EDUCATION
a) How this affects the patient: The patient requires additional help in school, especially in subjects like reading and math, as she struggles with speech delays and cognitive challenges.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 11) BEHAVIOUR AND DEVELOPMENT
a) How this affects the patient: The patient falls more often than other children, potentially indicating a neurological issue affecting balance or coordination.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 12) SKELETAL
a) How this affects the patient: The patient has an unusual structure of their spinal bones, leading to an increased curvature of the spine (scoliosis), and may experience delayed closure of the soft spot on the head (anterior fontanelle).
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 13) RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SCREENING AND TREATMENTS
a) Regular dental check-ups: To prevent tooth decay and ensure proper dental hygiene.
b) Regular hearing reviews to age 5: To detect and address hearing issues early.
c) Ophthalmology review: To monitor vision problems and ensure timely intervention.
d) Palate review: To assess speech and feeding difficulties, particularly if there are feeding or speech-related concerns.
e) Cardiac review: Including echocardiography and electrocardiogram (ECG) to rule out heart conditions.
f) Skeletal review: X-rays of the wrist, hips, spine, and skull to evaluate bone age and identify any abnormalities.
g) Monitoring growth velocity: To track height and weight, and refer for endocrine investigations if height is below the 2nd centile.
h) Physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, and behavioral therapy: To address physical, cognitive, and emotional challenges associated with KBG syndrome.

consultation:
Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s vision or eyes.
Parent: Our son has mentioned struggling to see the board at school, especially when the teacher writes in small letters or from a distance. We've noticed this issue for a while now, and it seems to affect his ability to follow lessons comfortably. He often squints or leans forward to get a better view.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child's hearing or ears.
Parent: There are times when our child doesn't respond immediately when called. It's as if he didn't hear us, even when we're standing right next to him. This has happened both at home and in quieter environments, so we're concerned it might be related to his hearing.

Doctor: Please tell us about the problems with your child’s teeth.
Parent: His teeth seem to break or chip very easily. Even minor accidents, like biting into something hard or a slight knock against another tooth, can cause damage. We've had to take him to the dentist more frequently than usual because of this issue.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s heart.
Parent: Yes, our child was born with a septal defect. We've been working closely with cardiologists to monitor the condition and ensure it doesn't worsen over time. So far, the treatments and lifestyle adjustments have helped manage the issue effectively.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child's hormones.
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about any neurological problem your child has (brain, nerves, muscle tone, fits).
Parent: Our child gets tired quickly during physical activity. Simple tasks like playing outside or running around with friends can leave him exhausted sooner than his peers. This has been noticeable since he started engaging in more active play.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child's kidneys.
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s immune system (ability to fight infection and vaccination responses).
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child’s gastrointestinal system (feeding, stomach, bowel).
Parent: Our child has a feeding aversion. Certain textures or smells of food can put him off completely. Mealtime can be challenging, and we've had to work with him to find foods he's comfortable eating.

Doctor: Please use this box to tell us about any other medical problems that you haven’t been able to mention above.
Parent: In addition to the issues already mentioned, our child seems behind other children in development. His fontanelle also took longer to close than typical, which was another concern we've been monitoring. These developmental delays and physical differences have required us to adapt his education and activities to better suit his needs.

# CLINICAL PATIENT REPORT

## 1) RESPIRATORY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: N/A

## 2) CARDIOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: Our child has a septal defect, which requires close monitoring and effective treatment to manage over time.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 38% of people with KBG syndrome have heart conditions, including changes to the heart valves, holes in the heart chambers, and structural changes.

## 3) GASTROENTEROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: Our child has a feeding aversion, making mealtime challenging and requiring adaptation to better suit his needs.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome struggle with swallowing and feeding difficulties, leading to frequent visits to the dentist and potential need for additional care.

## 4) IMMUNOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have seizures, which can be managed with standard anti-epileptic medications.

## 5) NEUROLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: Our child experiences fatigue during physical activity, particularly with more active play, affecting his overall energy levels.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome exhibit behavioral differences such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), or anxiety, which may require medication.

## 6) EAR NOSE THROAT
a) How this affects the patient: Our child struggles to see the board clearly at school, especially in smaller text or quiet environments, indicating possible hearing issues.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have recurrent otitis media or glue ear, which can lead to conductive hearing loss and speech delay.

## 7) OPHTHALMOLOGY AND VISION
a) How this affects the patient: Our child has vision problems such as astigmatism and short-sightedness/hypermetropia, which can worsen speech delay and make reading more challenging.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have vision problems, including astigmatism and short-sightedness/hypermetropia, which can impact communication and academic performance.

## 8) DERMATOLOGY
a) How this affects the patient: N/A
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have skin abnormalities, such as weak enamel and susceptibility to dental issues.

## 9) DENTAL
a) How this affects the patient: Our child requires frequent dental check-ups due to easy tooth breaks and chips, necessitating early intervention.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have dental issues, including broken or chipped teeth, and may need regular dental care.

## 10) EDUCATION
a) How this affects the patient: Our child faces challenges in adapting to the classroom environment, requiring modifications to meet his unique needs.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome show developmental delays and behavioral differences, impacting their educational progress.

## 11) BEHAVIOUR AND DEVELOPMENT
a) How this affects the patient: Our child exhibits fatigue during physical activity, particularly with more active play, affecting his overall energy levels.
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome display behavioral differences such as ASD, ADHD, or anxiety, which may require specialized interventions.

## 12) SKELETAL
a) How this affects the patient: Our child has an unusual structure of their spinal bones, potentially leading to an increased curvature of the spine (scoliosis), and short fingers with a curvature of the 5th finger (clinodactyly).
b) How this affects others with the syndrome: Around 20-40% of people with KBG syndrome have skeletal anomalies, including an unusual structure of their spinal bones, short fingers, and brachydactyly.

## 13) RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SCREENING AND TREATMENTS
a) Regular dental check-ups: To address the frequent tooth breaks and chips experienced by our child.
b) Regular hearing reviews to age 5: To monitor for otitis media or glue ear, which can cause conductive hearing loss and speech delay.
c) Ophthalmology review: To assess vision problems such as astigmatism and short-sightedness/hypermetropia, which can impact communication and academic performance.
d) Check position of testes in boys: To rule out cryptorchidism and ensure proper descent of testicles.
e) Consider a palate review: If there are feeding difficulties or speech concerns, referring for specialist review may be appropriate.
f) Referral for a cardiac review: Following diagnosis, ensuring effective management of the septal defect.
g) If nothing is found (or already done) this does not need to be repeated.
h) Consider a skeletal review: X-ray of the wrist (to determine bone age), hip, spine, and skull in children following diagnosis.
i) Any concerns around asymmetric hip creases in infancy and/or asymmetric or painful gait should prompt medical review.
j) Consider review and investigation for tethered cord (MRI) where clinical concerns arise on an individual basis (especially if sacral dimple is present).
k) Monitor growth velocity: If height is below the 2nd centile, refer for endocrine investigations on an individual basis and within context of familial heights.
l) Consider physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, and behavioral therapy to address the various challenges faced by our child.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s vision or eyes.
Parent: I'm worried about her eyesight because she always sits very close to the TV or when reading books. It's like she can't see things from a distance, and I fear it might affect her eyes in the long run.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child's hearing or ears.
Parent: Yes, she has otitis media. The doctor said it's an infection of the middle ear and we've been dealing with the consequences of that. 

Doctor: Please tell us about the problems with your child’s teeth.
Parent: Her teeth break or chip easily. Even a small fall or bump can cause damage. We've had to take extra care to ensure she doesn't hurt them further.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s heart.
Parent: She gets tired quickly when playing with friends or running around. It's hard for her to keep up with physical activities for long periods without needing a rest. This worries me because other kids seem to have more stamina.

Doctor: Please tell us about any neurological problem your child has (brain, nerves, muscle tone, fits).
Parent: Unfortunately, she has epilepsy. We have to be vigilant about her condition and ensure she takes her medication regularly to control the seizures. It's a constant concern for us.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child's kidneys.
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about any problems with your child’s immune system (ability to fight infection and vaccination responses).
Parent: N/A.

Doctor: Please tell us about problems with your child’s gastrointestinal system (feeding, stomach, bowel).
Parent: She's quite picky with food and often refuses to eat certain things. Mealtime can be challenging because of this, but we're working on introducing a variety of foods slowly.

Doctor: Please use this box to tell us about any other medical problems that you haven’t been able to mention above.
Parent: One thing that concerns me is her speech development. At four years old, I expected her to be talking more than she does now. The lack of speech is worrying me as it seems she's not meeting the expected milestone for her age.

Parent: N/A.
